projects.title: Millisecond Agent Sandboxes: Snapshot-Restored microVMs with a Credential-Injecting Proxy
projects.pitch: Rebuild a small version of Dropbox's agent runtime. Each conversation gets its own microVM, restored from a memory snapshot in milliseconds. The guest has no secrets. All outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy that checks permissions and injects credentials. You end up with an untrusted agent that can only reach files through a narrow, audited channel, plus rollback when it breaks something.
stack: JSON-RPC (threads/turns/items, modeled on Codex App Server)
you_will_learn: How VM snapshot/restore works: memory files, CoW disks, and why a restore beats a cold boot
Capability-based security: keeping secrets outside the trust boundary and injecting them at the proxy
Designing a policy enforcement point, and auditing every request an agent makes
Pool management: pre-warmed snapshots, sizing, and reclaim under memory pressure
Rollback by versioning file mutations, not by trusting the agent
milestones: Boot a minimal Linux guest in Firecracker and measure cold-boot latency
Take a post-init memory snapshot, restore it per session, and benchmark p50/p99 restore time
Mount a per-session copy-on-write workspace via virtio-fs or rclone and verify isolation between sessions
Build the host proxy: allowlisted destinations, per-session scoped tokens injected into headers, and a structured audit log
Expose a JSON-RPC API (thread → turn → item) and run a CLI agent inside the VM through it
Add plan approval (the proxy blocks writes until a plan is approved) and one-click rollback using file version history
Load test 50 concurrent sessions on one host and graph restore latency vs. memory overcommit

projects.title: Amplification Lab: A Tiny LSM Tree and B-Tree with Read/Write/Space Amplification Meters
projects.pitch: Write two small key-value engines behind the same interface, an LSM tree and a copy-on-write B-tree. Instrument every physical byte they read and write. Then run the same workloads against both and see the read, write, and space amplification tradeoffs in your own numbers. Finally, change one variable at a time (Bloom filters, compaction strategy, compression, block cache) and measure the effect.
stack: io_uring (optional) or direct pread/pwrite with O_DIRECT
Grafana or a Jupyter notebook for plots
you_will_learn: Read, write, and space amplification as physical cost per logical operation
Memtables, WAL, SSTables, and leveled vs. tiered compaction
B-tree page splits, fill factor, and why random writes hurt
Bloom filter false-positive math and its effect on point lookups
Block cache sizing and its effect on read amplification
milestones: Define a KV interface and a byte-counting I/O layer that every engine must use
Build the LSM: WAL, skiplist memtable, flush to immutable SSTables, and naive point lookup
Add leveled compaction, then tiered compaction, and record write amplification for each
Build a page-based B-tree with splits and a simple buffer pool
Write YCSB-style workloads (A/B/C/E) and generate amplification and throughput charts
Add Bloom filters, compression, and an LRU block cache one at a time and record each delta
Write up when you would pick each engine, backed by your own numbers

projects.title: Laggard: A Multiplexing Proxy for Terrible Links, Tested Against a Simulated GEO Satellite
projects.pitch: Build a local and remote proxy pair that hides 600 ms+ RTT links. It keeps warm, long-lived TCP connections open, multiplexes many app streams over them, terminates TLS on the ground side to save handshake round trips, and compresses traffic. Use netem to emulate in-flight Wi-Fi, then measure how much each technique actually saves in page-load time.
stack: yamux-style framing or QUIC (quinn / quic-go) for comparison
you_will_learn: Why handshake round trips dominate on high-latency links, and how connection warming hides them
Stream multiplexing and TCP head-of-line blocking, compared against QUIC
Congestion control: CUBIC vs. BBR under loss and large bandwidth-delay products
Flow control and backpressure across multiplexed streams so one large download can't starve the others
Security tradeoffs of terminating TLS at a trusted relay
milestones: Build a netem testbed: 600 ms RTT, 1% loss, 5 Mbps, with a client and server in separate namespaces
Baseline: measure time-to-first-byte and full page load with direct HTTPS
Build a SOCKS5 local proxy that tunnels over a single pre-warmed TCP connection to a remote relay
Add stream multiplexing with per-stream flow-control windows and show fairness between a large and a small transfer
Terminate TLS at the relay so new origins cost one RTT on the long link; add streaming zstd
Switch congestion control between CUBIC and BBR, and replace the transport with QUIC; chart all variants
Add metrics for in-flight bytes, stream window stalls, and RTT, plus a Grafana dashboard

projects.title: Emoji Storm: A WebSocket Fanout Server That Survives Thundering Herds, Plus Its Own Koi Pond
projects.pitch: Build a Slack-like channel fanout service, then a load generator that opens 100k+ WebSocket connections and fires reaction storms at a huge channel. Watch the naive design fall over. Then fix it with coalescing, batching, per-client backpressure, and slow-consumer eviction, measuring each step.
stack: NATS or Redis Streams for pub/sub
Custom load generator spread across several network namespaces / IPs
you_will_learn: Fanout cost: O(members × events) and why reactions in large channels are a worst case
Event coalescing and debounced aggregation (send '+37 :tada:' instead of 37 messages)
Backpressure: bounded per-connection send queues, drop policies, and evicting slow consumers
Thundering herds on reconnect: jittered backoff and admission control
Building a load tester that is itself scalable: ephemeral port exhaustion, file descriptor limits, kernel tuning
milestones: Build a minimal channel server: join, post, and react, with fanout over pub/sub
Build a load generator that holds 100k idle WebSocket connections (tune ulimit, ip_local_port_range, multiple source IPs)
Run a storm of 1,000 reactions per second into a 50k-member channel; record p99 delivery latency and memory before it collapses
Add per-channel reaction coalescing on 100 ms windows and compare message volume and latency
Add bounded send queues with drop-oldest for ephemeral events, and evict consumers that stay slow
Kill the server mid-storm and add jittered reconnect plus a token-bucket admission gate to avoid a reconnect herd
Publish dashboards and a short report comparing each mitigation

projects.title: Autoloop Lite: A Durable Background Agent Runner That Only Pings You When Unsure
projects.pitch: Build a small durable-execution engine for CLI coding agents. Tasks are queued, leased to workers, checkpointed after every step, and resumed after crashes. A confidence and risk gate decides whether an action runs automatically or becomes an approval card sent to your phone. The focus is the reliability engineering underneath agent workflows, not the agent itself.
stack: SQLite in WAL mode or Postgres with SKIP LOCKED
Any CLI agent (Claude Code, Codex CLI, aider) as a subprocess
Web Push or ntfy for approval cards
you_will_learn: Lease-based work queues: visibility timeouts, heartbeats, and handling a worker that dies holding a lease
Durable execution through event sourcing and deterministic replay of step history
Idempotency keys so retried side effects (git push, PR comments) happen once
Policy gating: classifying actions by risk and blocking on human approval without holding resources
Tracing long-running, multi-hour workflows end to end
milestones: Design the schema: tasks, leases, a step event log, and approvals; implement claim with SKIP LOCKED or an atomic SQLite update
Run an agent subprocess per task and log every tool call and output as an append-only event
kill -9 the worker mid-task and resume from the last checkpoint by replaying events
Wrap side-effecting tools with idempotency keys and verify that duplicate retries are no-ops
Add a risk policy (read = auto, write to repo = auto, push or network = approval) and send approval cards via ntfy
Have blocked tasks park without holding a worker, and wake on approval
Add OpenTelemetry spans per task and step, plus a dashboard of queue depth, lease expiries, and approval wait time
